title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool to allocate, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: A 12-year hardware company founder explains the concrete mechanics of org rewrite: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs land — with details and pitfalls.
who: Founders, HR leaders and business heads pushing AI org transformation, especially in hardware or consumer electronics companies who want to move the org but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native org is not ‘everyone should use AI well’, but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and try not to have people do it. The more radical step is to assume the original org and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes, but tearing them down first and rebuilding. He admits this mainly targets core org builders, not slogans for everyone.

points.h: HARO's lead comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it's different from ordinary HR+IT: the lead must understand the business, and they chose an old partner who co-founded with him and has done tech, product, CEO, R&D, brand, and IT. The logic is reversed — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI; now a tech-oriented person leads, and they give him HR BPs who are sensitive to people. Under this department there is a solid-line AIO (the former IT team, future Agent Builder), and a dotted-line FDE.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people short-term
points.body: Chen Bin draws a clear distinction: Agent Builder leans technical, can build an Agent; FDE must go into the business front line, sort out supply, planning, procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long-term one person might handle it, but short-term two kinds of people must work together. They didn't copy Anker's approach of pulling people out for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead they let business people spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI transformation while doing business. The company also set up AI levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI navigators’, and above that ‘pilots’.

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads get the bonus pool
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and Huawei's matrix: the matrix is product line and function dual-line, while a circle is a small team with an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries, making the circle lead more powerful. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it, even how much to give himself; HR and functional departments only have advisory power. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates, and the functional line may become something like a technical committee in the future, but within half a year to a year of transformation, let the front line decide first.

Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from their university days in 2023, have no fear in doing things, and use it more than veterans. His exact words are ‘sometimes experience becomes a burden’, and the most troublesome are the half-baked — experience hasn't arrived but they think they're very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as a foundation, but which processes and roles can be removed is easier for clear-headed people to judge. The threshold for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill use and Agent building; only L3 can write workflows.

points.h: R&D transforms fast, marketing transforms slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits transformation speeds vary greatly by department: technical R&D related to software and coding is easiest, with daily code writing giving positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and bonus increases. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not improve quality, and 60-point work doesn't stick. His response is to make everyone think like a business operator: whether content can bring conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three rounds of internal sign-ups: the first round for incremental roles, such as a dozen or so company-level Agents and corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second round for roles missing after circles formed, such as content marketing Agent Builders; the third round continued to fill. Applicants first do a self-assessment to discover what they're good at, then a three-to-five-minute defense, and after judges score, AI is used to analyze meeting minutes and speeches for matching. A hundred applicants might end up with twenty or thirty selected. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

points.h: Hiring requires proving AI can't do the job
points.body: After people from original departments were picked by circles, when a boss wanted to add headcount, logically there were only two channels: find AI management trainees, or use more AI tokens. If they really must rehire, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and they must explain why they can't use management trainees and why they can't use AI. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, CHO as a service, working with Chen Bin on the AI-native transformation.

points.h: IPD is not overturned, only accelerated
points.body: Chen Bin says he is actually the most radical one in the company, often held back by others asking for more caution. Regarding Huawei IPD and similar accumulations, his judgment is: AI can only transform processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, from strategy to execution, SP to BP, originally took three months to half a year, now two months, doubling efficiency, but the nodes like five looks and three settings remain, just originally three weeks now three days. Training a product line manager originally took 10 to 15 years, now three to five years, but the rotation positions that should be rotated cannot be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three types of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature before choosing, with lower trial-and-error costs. But the more cutting-edge the tech company, the earlier they should embrace AI, because technology changes greatly and markets change fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically mentions that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and similar should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are more channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly create a feedback loop from user end to supply chain end, with greater effect.

quotes.text: I think a native org may first start from AI — what can AI do, try not to have people do it, think AI-native first, think about this thing, even this process, logically should be restructured.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm end-to-end, a small team with a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or boundaries, make functional power smaller, make the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience becomes a burden; it's better to have it, but often the half-baked are scary — their experience hasn't arrived but they think they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

We try to fill with AI, right? Prioritize using AI, use AI to fill what can be filled, unless it can't be filled; if it can't be filled, then internally we say either you find AI management trainees to fill it, or use more AI tokens.

Originally it might take at least three months to half a year, now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least doubled efficiency, but the process itself hasn't changed, it's just that I used to have five meetings, now three meetings, two meetings.

Actually look at the real value AI brings in this industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it may bring, indeed lower; if lower, then you can reasonably say you can wait until these — like us who are digging pits and playing, right? Or like Doubao, Volcano Engine, these doing better — then you choose, it's fine.
